rules.statement: Never derive an issuer, base address or any published absolute URL from the incoming request (scheme, `Host` header, path base or route); build them only from the configured or stored issuer.
rules.why: A request-derived origin lets a caller's `Host` header choose where the server tells clients to send their credentials, and keeps a second materialization path alive.
rules.check: Look for `HttpRequest.Host`, `Scheme`, `PathBase` or `UriHelper.BuildAbsolute`/`GetDisplayUrl` used to build issuer values, discovery metadata, endpoint URLs, redirect targets or bootstrap documents.

rules.statement: Do not add a public option, flag or opt-in that weakens a security control below its safe baseline, not even one meant only for development; the default must be safe and must not be configurable down.
rules.why: Correct-by-default: every library consumer inherits an unsafe fallback until they configure otherwise, and a production-safety gate that reads configuration cannot see runtime-written data.
rules.check: Look for new options such as `AllowX`, `UseRequestHost`, `DisableValidation` or development-only switches that bypass a security check or fall back to an insecure behavior.

rules.statement: When a stored entity is missing a value its security identity depends on (such as a tenant's issuer), fail closed instead of filling it in from the request or some other ambient fallback.
rules.why: An entity with no authoritative identity must not be served under an address someone else picked.
rules.check: Look for null-coalescing or fallback branches that replace a missing stored identity value with a request-derived or ambient value at serve time.

rules.statement: Persist a defaulted identity value (such as an issuer expanded from a template) when the entity is written; do not re-derive it each time it is read or each time a request arrives.
rules.why: Relying parties configure the issuer, so re-deriving it would move every existing entity whenever a template or default changed.
rules.check: Look for code that computes an issuer or other identity value from a template or option on each read or request instead of reading the stored value.

rules.statement: On every write path (create, update, provisioning), apply the default for an omitted value first and then run the same validation used for explicit values, so a derived value is judged exactly like a supplied one.
rules.why: If a derived value skipped validation, it could produce an address the strategy cannot serve or one that collides with a reserved address.
rules.check: Look for write paths that fill a default after validation runs, that skip validation for defaulted values, or that apply defaulting on some write paths but not others.

rules.statement: Validate configured URI templates and the addresses they expand to when the host starts (for example with `ValidateOnStart`), not when they are first used.
rules.why: A malformed template, or one whose expansion its strategy cannot serve, should stop the host at startup and not show up later as a tenant that cannot be written or served.
rules.check: Look for new template or address options that do not have startup validation of their syntax (such as an exact single variable) and of a probe expansion.

rules.statement: Do not add literal action segments under a collection route whose next segment is a resource identifier (such as `/api/tenants/check-address`); expose the operation as a sub-resource of the resource it describes.
rules.why: A literal segment under the collection collides with a resource of that name, and a sub-resource cannot collide.
rules.check: Look for new routes of the form `/api/{collection}/{literal}` next to an existing `/api/{collection}/{id}` route.

rules.statement: A preview or dry-run endpoint must call the same validation seam as the write it previews, and must authorize as a read when the resource exists and as a create when it does not.
rules.why: Then the preview's verdict matches what the write will decide, and the preview cannot be used to bypass create authorization.
rules.check: Look for preview endpoints that duplicate validation logic instead of calling the write path's validator, or that use one fixed authorization policy whether or not the resource exists.
